content: Erosion is the process by which earth materials are worn away and transported by natural forces such as water, wind, ice, and gravity. Water erosionâthe most widespread typeâoccurs through several mechanisms: rainsplash dislodges soil particles upon impact; sheet erosion removes thin layers of soil in overland flow; rill erosion creates small channels; and gully erosion forms larger channels through concentrated flow. Stream erosion depends on water velocity and sediment load, with faster water generally causing more erosion and streams eventually carving characteristic landforms like valleys, floodplains, and oxbow lakes. Wind erosion becomes significant in arid regions with sparse vegetation and dry, loose soil. Wind removes lighter particles through suspension (dust) and saltation (bouncing sand grains), creating features like dunes and deflation hollows. Gravity directly moves material downslope through mass wasting processes ranging from gradual soil creep to catastrophic landslides, with slope steepness and material cohesion determining movement type and rate. Glacial erosion occurs as flowing ice incorporates and transports material, scraping and plucking underlying bedrock to create distinctive U-shaped valleys, cirques, and moraines. Erosion rates depend on multiple factors: climate (precipitation intensity and frequency), topography (slope steepness and length), soil properties (texture, structure, organic content), vegetation cover (roots bind soil and reduce raindrop impact), and human activities (deforestation, agriculture, construction). While erosion naturally shapes landscapes over geological time, accelerated erosion from human disturbance can cause environmental problems including soil degradation, water quality impairment, infrastructure damage, and habitat destruction.

scenario.title: Terrain Transformation Lab
scenario.content: Students create and manipulate virtual landscapes in a sandbox environment, then observe how different erosive forces reshape the terrain. The simulation allows students to build landforms, adjust material properties, and apply various erosional agents including rainfall, flowing water, wind, and gravity. The system visualizes erosion in real-time, showing soil particle movement, channel formation, and landform evolution across accelerated timescales. Students can measure erosion rates, sediment transport, and deposition patterns while experimenting with protective measures like vegetation, terracing, and windbreaks. Interactive tools allow students to switch between perspectivesâfrom ground-level observation to overhead mapping viewsâand create cross-sections revealing subsurface changes. Challenge scenarios task students with managing erosion in different contexts (agricultural fields, coastal areas, construction sites) or predicting landscape evolution under changing climate conditions, teaching both natural processes and conservation practices.

hypothesis.description: Students will compare erosion mechanisms by analyzing how different forces move earth materials. They will predict how landscape features respond to various erosional processes, and explain how natural and human factors influence erosion rates and patterns.
